theme: The brief that never shows up in the brief

linkedin.text:
I've read thousands of event briefs over 16 years.

Most of them are precise about logistics and vague about what actually matters: the energy in the room at the end of the night. The thing the CEO wants people to carry home. The quiet signal to a team that they're valued.

That unwritten brief? It's usually the hardest to execute — and the only one people remember.

Senior planners: how do you surface the real goal in the first client conversation? Curious what works for others.

instagram.text:
The brief said: 400 people, Lisbon, three days, gala on the last night.

What the brief didn't say: this team hadn't been in the same room in four years. The merger had been rough. Leadership needed the room to feel like one company again — not just look like it.

That's the actual job. And it's almost never written down.

If you're planning something for your team and you're not sure how to put that part into words yet — that's exactly where the conversation should start. DM me. 🎯

facebook.text:
Every client hands us a brief. Venue, date, headcount, budget. What almost no brief mentions — but what every event actually lives or dies by — is the feeling the room needs to hold at 9pm when the speeches are done and the real conversations start.

After 1,500+ events across 130+ destinations, that's the question I ask first now: What do you need people to feel when the agenda runs out?

What's been the hardest thing to put into words when you've planned an event? Drop it in the comments.
